s: Baroque anchor on Vienna's skyline, named for a reformer
w: A Baroque set piece straddling the line between Wieden and the Innere Stadt, dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, one of the Counter-Reformation's leading figures. Close enough to Vienna's centre that it's impossible to miss on the skyline, even if the man it honours needs more of an introduction.
_facts: Baroque church in the Karlsplatz, Vienna, Austria
Dedicated to Saint Charles Borromeo, a leading figure of the Counter-Reformation
Located on the border of Wieden and the Innere Stadt, the city centre

s: Home turf of the Vienna Philharmonic since 1870
w: Built on land Emperor Franz Joseph I granted to the Society of Friends of Music during 1863 construction of the Ringstrasse, this Theophil Hansen hall has housed the Vienna Philharmonic since opening in 1870. Its Great Hall's acoustics rank with Amsterdam's Concertgebouw and Boston's Symphony Hall.
_facts: Concert hall in the Innere Stadt district, Vienna
Land granted to the Society of Friends of Music by Franz Joseph I during 1863 Ringstrasse construction
Designed by Theophil Hansen; has housed the Vienna Philharmonic since opening in 1870
Great Hall's acoustics ranked alongside Concertgebouw (Amsterdam) and Symphony Hall (Boston)

s: One name, two places: parkland and a fairground inside it
w: Six square kilometres of public parkland fill Leopoldstadt, Vienna's 2nd district, though say 'the Prater' to a local and they'll likely picture just one corner of it: the Wurstelprater, the amusement park tucked inside the wider green sprawl. Everybody defaults to the fairground over the trees.
_facts: 6 km2 public park in Vienna's 2nd district, Leopoldstadt
The name Prater is often used to refer to the Wurstelprater, an amusement park within the area
